entities.summary:
Domenico Colombo (died 1497) was a Genoese wool weaver and small-time merchant whose primary historical significance stems from his paternity of the celebrated explorer Christopher Columbus and his lesser-known but equally adventurous brother, Bartholomew Columbus. Living in the bustling maritime Republic of Genoa during the 15th century, Domenico's life was characterized by a modest artisan's existence, far removed from the grand voyages and geopolitical shifts his sons would later instigate. His trajectory from a relatively stable artisan to one frequently embroiled in debt provides a microhistorical lens into the economic pressures faced by the working and lower-middle classes of late medieval Italian city-states.

Born into a family that had some landholdings in Moconesi, Domenico established himself in Genoa as a master weaver. His marriage to Susanna Fontanarossa around 1445-1450 produced at least five children, including Christopher (born c. 1451) and Bartholomew (born c. 1461). He operated a weaving workshop and also engaged in innkeeping and cheese selling, often struggling with financial solvency. Records show him moving between Genoa and Savona, seeking better economic opportunities, and frequently being involved in lawsuits over debts, underscoring the precariousness of his ventures despite his skilled trade.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Domenico Colombo's significance lies not in his personal achievements but as the father of Christopher Columbus, whose voyages initiated the Columbian Exchange and the Age of Exploration, fundamentally reshaping global history. His life provides a window into the economic realities of 15th-century Genoese artisans and the familial origins of world-changing figures.
